Moonshot

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
One woman. One idea. One shot at the Moon.

Unique Selling Point:
Moonshot – Race to the Moon
There’s a new global space race underway — between the United States, China, Russia… and unexpectedly, South Africa. But this time, the race isn’t about planting flags or sending astronauts. It’s about turning the Moon into a giant listening device using Radio Astronomy Telescopes — capable of detecting signals from the very beginning of the universe. Scientists believe the Moon could hold the key to answering some of the biggest unanswered questions in physics: How did the universe begin? What is dark matter? And are we alone?
The reason everyone is trying to do this? Lies in a simple problem: Earth is noisy. Our atmosphere blocks certain radio signals travelling through space, and billions of electronic devices generate constant interference. In other words, scientists are trying to hear a whisper… in the middle of a stadium. But just 384,000 kilometres away, the Moon offers something unique: silence.
With no atmosphere and minimal interference, it provides a rare opportunity to detect faint signals that have travelled billions of years — clues to what astronomers call “first light,” the moment the first stars formed after the Big Bang. At the centre of this mission is Carla Mitchell, an unlikely space pioneer based in Cape Town. Not an astrophysicist, but an economist working at the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, Carla has spent more than a decade chasing an idea many believed was impossible: placing radio astronomy instruments on the Moon.
Her solution is deceptively simple. Instead of one massive telescope, Carla has designed small, spherical antennas — each about 30 centimetres wide — that can survive the unpredictable conditions of lunar landing. She calls them “Moon B.A.L.L.S.” — Bounced African Low Lunar Spheres. The design solves one of space exploration’s biggest challenges: landing. Traditional instruments can fail if they tip or land incorrectly. A sphere works no matter how it touches down.
Her long-term vision is bold: to place dozens of these spheres across the Moon’s surface, allowing them to work together as a single, powerful telescope array — potentially the first of its kind on another world. And the ideal location? The far side of the Moon. Because the Moon is tidally locked, one side always faces Earth. The far side never does — making it naturally shielded from our planet’s radio noise, and one of the quietest places in the solar system.



Summary:
But getting there has always been the challenge: Lunar missions cost hundreds of millions of dollars — far beyond the reach of most research teams.
Until now.
In 2023, China issued a global call for scientific experiments to join its future lunar programme. Countries around the world applied — including South Africa. After two years of evaluation, Carla’s Africa2Moon project was selected to fly on China’s Chang’e-8 mission, scheduled for 2029. The prize: a free ride to the Moon.
For the first time, South Africa will be able to send scientific instruments into space at no launch cost — turning Carla’s decade-long vision into a real mission. But the opportunity comes with pressure.
At SARAO in Observatory, Cape Town, Carla and her team are now racing to assemble and test the first Moon Ball prototypes. Budgets are tight, timelines are critical, and much of the work relies on collaboration, donated components, and determination. Carte Blanche has secured access to this project at a pivotal moment — as Carla’s idea moves from theory to reality. We would have a front row seat to the assembly and go with a presenter to meet the team. Carla says we can go to the top of the telescope and do an interview with the presenter looking at the moon, while discussing her dream.
“People imagine huge telescopes,” Carla explains. “But our instruments are small. The Moon Balls are about thirty centimetres across — simple spherical antennas that can work no matter how they land.”
For this initial mission, only three of the spherical antennas will be sent — a proof of concept. If successful, it could pave the way for a much larger array on future missions. With visuals from SARAO and the SKA telescope array (which Carte Blanche has reported on before), alongside NASA’s lunar archive and international launch footage, the story offers both scale and intimacy: a global race to the Moon… driven by one woman’s persistence. Because if this mission succeeds, Carla Mitchell’s small metal spheres — built in a lab in Cape Town — could help humanity listen back to the very first moments of the universe.
“The first words spoken by God in the Bible are ‘Let there be light.’ In a way, that’s what we’re looking for — the first light in the universe, the first stars being born. One of the most exciting discoveries in radio astronomy is about trying to detect what we call ‘first light.’”
And after more than a decade chasing the idea, she still looks up at the Moon with the same thought.
“Sometimes I look up at the Moon and think — my balls are going to be there one day. I’ve been praying for this on my knees for years.”
And in doing so, mark Africa’s first step onto another world.

Script:


(Catherine) On a quiet night in Cape Town… a woman looks up at the night sky, and ponders the mysteries it holds…
(Neil Armstrong) One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
(Carla) My kind of worship is discovery. And so I look to understand the universe and I that inspires us at a very deep level...
It feels impossible to get my balls from here to the moon.
(Catherine) Moonballs: a concept name that at first sounds absurd, could become key to a great discovery; our next “great leap”.
(Catherine link) And unexpectedly… South Africa is leading the way! This time, the goal is to place a specialised telescope on the moon that listens to space and will answer questions like How did the universe begin? What is dark matter? And are we alone?
(Catherine) These questions are what drive Dr Carla Mitchell. Who surprisingly isn’t an astrophysicist.
(Carla) I'm actually an economist and I'm an average person, and I'm putting a telescope on the moon.
(Catherine) Well you don't seem very average to me.
(Carla) People in the space industry have told me my knowledge doesn't constrain me because I'm not in a particular field, so it helps me to join dots that maybe other people haven't seen.
(Catherine) Carla’s mission is to put a telescope on the moon - but it’s probably not the type you’re imagining. Not all telescopes are the same. This optical telescope — over 150 years old — looks at visible light.
(Catherine) But the one Carla wants to send to the Moon detects wavelengths we can’t see. Stars, galaxies, comets - they all emit invisible signals — radio waves — which radio telescopes detect.
(Carla) We're searching for these signals and receiving them like a radio would. So we loosely say we're listening to the universe in radio astronomy. And then that data we receive, we convert into images.
(Catherine) The MeerKAT radio telescope - a sequence of 64 interlinked radio dishes in the Karoo- is one of the world’s most powerful. It detects a wide range of wavelengths. When scientists assign colours to the different signals, they transform the raw data into breathtaking images.
(Catherine) But there’s a problem: Earth is noisy. Signals from technology crowd the airwaves - and our own atmosphere acts as a silencer, interfering with the signals received from deep space.
(Catherine) Theoretical Physicist, Dr Adriana Marais explains that the lowest, faintest signals are blocked before they can even reach us.
(Adriana) So between 0 and 20 megahertz are signals that don't make it through our ionosphere because they are either reflected or interfered with by our atmosphere on Earth.
(Catherine) But there’s a place… where that noise can’t interfere.
(Catherine link) If you’re trying to hear a whisper you don’t stay in a crowded room. You go somewhere quiet. And in space that place is the far side of the moon.
(Catherine) But getting there… is another challenge.
(Catherine) So, Carla founded Africa2Moon and partnered with Adriana’s Foundation for Space Development Africa.
(Adriana) As the story goes, what do you get when you cross an economist looking to positively impact lives in Africa with a quantum biologist looking to life on Mars? And the answer is obviously Africa's first Moon mission.
(Carla) So Africa2Moon is like my child. I've been working on it for 13 years. And it's really a dream to put the first radio astronomy array onto the lunar surface.
(Adriana) As of yet, no one has managed to successfully do radio astronomy from the far side of the Moon, and what we hope is to really show the way of a new kind of technology that can be more robust, is low cost, is low mass, and can reveal aspects of the universe that we haven't yet been able to detect.
(Catherine) But Moon dust is razor-sharp and its lunar terrain is unpredictable. Even billion-dollar missions have failed to land here. A radically new design was needed.
(Carla) So the idea behind the moonballs was looking at the challenges that other missions have faced, you know, with legs collapsing or their solar panels pointing the wrong way, etc. And trying to find a solution that wasn't dependent on how it landed.
(Catherine) And as Carla looked up at the Moon, trying to solve that problem… she saw the answer in its shape.
(Carla) Well, a ball that seemed obvious to me at the time. And so I thought, well, a ball doesn't matter how it rolls, it can bounce. And so that eliminated a lot of the risk.
(Carla) So balls stands for Bounced African Low Lunar Spheres.
(Catherine) Africa2Moon has many partners — including our own Radio Astronomy Observatory, SARAO — which runs the country’s radio telescopes.
(Catherine) Local industry and universities donated the parts and provided engineering skills and students to work on the project — helping design, build, and test the technology. SARAO’s lead engineer, Thomas Kusel.
(Catherine) When Carla came up with this concept and this idea, what was your response?
(Thomas) Well, I First thought she's crazy … because there's so many technical challenges to getting it done. We relied a lot on our experience on previous projects in SARAO to be able to structure this from a crazy idea to an actual thing that can be launched.
(Keitumetse) You need a design that can sustain the terrain that can be easily deployed.
The telescopes we put out in the Karoo are huge. For you to be able to send one of those on a rocket, you can imagine the size of the rocket that you need to build. So we had to be very innovative.
(Catherine) This led to the first prototype - which is only 30cm in diameter!
(Catherine) But there was another problem. Getting to the Moon.
(Catherine link) It sounds simple. Put a telescope on the moon. But, that’s exactly where the challenge begins. Because getting there is one thing, landing is something else entirely.
(Catherine) Then, three years ago, China invited the world to apply to join a new lunar mission.
(Catherine) Their Chang’e-8 mission — planned for 2029 — is part of a broader effort to explore the Lunar South Pole and lay the groundwork for a future Moon base.
(Thomas) We just put together a proposal, a conceptual design and to our delight we were accepted on the Chang'e-8 programme.
(Carla) I've never felt so small in my life when I realised it was actually going to happen.
(Catherine) So your Moonballs are basically hitching a free ride to the Moon?
(Carla) Absolutely and China has extended a hand in collaboration more than anyone else.
(Catherine) This was their ‘one small step’ — but now they had just 13 months to make their first three working Moonballs.
(Carla) We're actually being attached to the outside of the lander. So we have a lot more of an extreme environment to survive all the way to the Moon. It ultimately came to what it looks like today, just the rings, hollow, with the electronics inside.
(Catherine) On paper, Earth2Moon has cost almost nothing. But in expertise, time and technology… It's worth around R1.4 billion.
(Catherine) So this project hasn't cost much money at all?
(Adriana) I think as Carla says, she's bought a few pizzas for the team but that's it.
(Carla) 33 scientists and engineers volunteered their free time. The most recent, US mission, cost 120 million dollars.
(Catherine link) For now its just three small spheres, But if they work they could change how we view the universe..forever
(Catherine) Africa2Moon hopes to send 55 in total — spread across the Moon and working together as one giant radio telescope.
(Catherine) Because in space… distance is time. The Moonballs could detect signals billions of years old — from our Sun, our galaxy, and beyond.
(Carla) So shortly after the Big Bang, the Universe was a hot mess, and the very first stars began to form. So we would be looking to detect the very first light in the Universe.

(Carla) My kind of worship is discovery. And so I look to understand the universe and I that inspires us at a very deep level... It feels impossible to get my balls from here to the moon. (Catherine) Moonballs: a concept name that at first sounds absurd, could become key to a great discovery; our next “great leap”. (Catherine link) And unexpectedly… South Africa is leading the way! This time, the goal is to place a specialised telescope on the moon that listens to space and will answer questions like How did the universe begin? What is dark matter? And are we alone? (Catherine) These questions are what drive Dr Carla Mitchell. Who surprisingly isn’t an astrophysicist. (Carla) I'm actually an economist and I'm an average person, and I'm putting a telescope on the moon. (Catherine) Well you don't seem very average to me. (Carla) People in the space industry have told me my knowledge doesn't constrain me because I'm not in a particular field, so it helps me to join dots that maybe other people haven't seen. (Catherine) Carla’s mission is to put a telescope on the moon - but it’s probably not the type you’re imagining. Not all telescopes are the same. This optical telescope — over 150 years old — looks at visible light. (Catherine) But the one Carla wants to send to the Moon detects wavelengths we can’t see. Stars, galaxies, comets - they all emit invisible signals — radio waves — which radio telescopes detect. (Carla) We're searching for these signals and receiving them like a radio would. So we loosely say we're listening to the universe in radio astronomy. And then that data we receive, we convert into images. (Catherine) The MeerKAT radio telescope - a sequence of 64 interlinked radio dishes in the Karoo- is one of the world’s most powerful. It detects a wide range of wavelengths. When scientists assign colours to the different signals, they transform the raw data into breathtaking images. (Catherine) But there’s a problem: Earth is noisy. Signals from technology crowd the airwaves - and our own atmosphere acts as a silencer, interfering with the signals received from deep space. (Catherine) Theoretical Physicist, Dr Adriana Marais explains that the lowest, faintest signals are blocked before they can even reach us. (Adriana) So between 0 and 20 megahertz are signals that don't make it through our ionosphere because they are either reflected or interfered with by our atmosphere on Earth. (Catherine) But there’s a place… where that noise can’t interfere. (Catherine link) If you’re trying to hear a whisper you don’t stay in a crowded room. You go somewhere quiet. And in space that place is the far side of the moon. (Catherine) But getting there… is another challenge. (Catherine) So, Carla founded Africa2Moon and partnered with Adriana’s Foundation for Space Development Africa. (Adriana) As the story goes, what do you get when you cross an economist looking to positively impact lives in Africa with a quantum biologist looking to life on Mars? And the answer is obviously Africa's first Moon mission. (Carla) So Africa2Moon is like my child. I've been working on it for 13 years. And it's really a dream to put the first radio astronomy array onto the lunar surface. (Adriana) As of yet, no one has managed to successfully do radio astronomy from the far side of the Moon, and what we hope is to really show the way of a new kind of technology that can be more robust, is low cost, is low mass, and can reveal aspects of the universe that we haven't yet been able to detect. (Catherine) But Moon dust is razor-sharp and its lunar terrain is unpredictable. Even billion-dollar missions have failed to land here. A radically new design was needed. (Carla) So the idea behind the moonballs was looking at the challenges that other missions have faced, you know, with legs collapsing or their solar panels pointing the wrong way, etc. And trying to find a solution that wasn't dependent on how it landed. (Catherine) And as Carla looked up at the Moon, trying to solve that problem… she saw the answer in its shape. (Carla) Well, a ball that seemed obvious to me at the time. And so I thought, well, a ball doesn't matter how it rolls, it can bounce. And so that eliminated a lot of the risk. (Carla) So balls stands for Bounced African Low Lunar Spheres. (Catherine) Africa2Moon has many partners — including our own Radio Astronomy Observatory, SARAO — which runs the country’s radio telescopes. (Catherine) Local industry and universities donated the parts and provided engineering skills and students to work on the project — helping design, build, and test the technology. SARAO’s lead engineer, Thomas Kusel. (Catherine) When Carla came up with this concept and this idea, what was your response? (Thomas) Well, I First thought she's crazy … because there's so many technical challenges to getting it done. We relied a lot on our experience on previous projects in SARAO to be able to structure this from a crazy idea to an actual thing that can be launched. (Keitumetse) You need a design that can sustain the terrain that can be easily deployed. The telescopes we put out in the Karoo are huge. For you to be able to send one of those on a rocket, you can imagine the size of the rocket that you need to build. So we had to be very innovative. (Catherine) This led to the first prototype - which is only 30cm in diameter! (Catherine) But there was another problem. Getting to the Moon. (Catherine link) It sounds simple. Put a telescope on the moon. But, that’s exactly where the challenge begins. Because getting there is one thing, landing is something else entirely. (Catherine) Then, three years ago, China invited the world to apply to join a new lunar mission. (Catherine) Their Chang’e-8 mission — planned for 2029 — is part of a broader effort to explore the Lunar South Pole and lay the groundwork for a future Moon base. (Thomas) We just put together a proposal, a conceptual design and to our delight we were accepted on the Chang'e-8 programme. (Carla) I've never felt so small in my life when I realised it was actually going to happen. (Catherine) So your Moonballs are basically hitching a free ride to the Moon? (Carla) Absolutely and China has extended a hand in collaboration more than anyone else. (Catherine) This was their ‘one small step’ — but now they had just 13 months to make their first three working Moonballs. (Carla) We're actually being attached to the outside of the lander. So we have a lot more of an extreme environment to survive all the way to the Moon. It ultimately came to what it looks like today, just the rings, hollow, with the electronics inside. (Catherine) On paper, Earth2Moon has cost almost nothing. But in expertise, time and technology… It's worth around R1.4 billion. (Catherine) So this project hasn't cost much money at all? (Adriana) I think as Carla says, she's bought a few pizzas for the team but that's it. (Carla) 33 scientists and engineers volunteered their free time. The most recent, US mission, cost 120 million dollars. (Catherine link) For now its just three small spheres, But if they work they could change how we view the universe..forever (Catherine) Africa2Moon hopes to send 55 in total — spread across the Moon and working together as one giant radio telescope. (Catherine) Because in space… distance is time. The Moonballs could detect signals billions of years old — from our Sun, our galaxy, and beyond. (Carla) So shortly after the Big Bang, the Universe was a hot mess, and the very first stars began to form. So we would be looking to detect the very first light in the Universe.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): One woman. One idea. One shot at the Moon.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Moonshot – Race to the Moon There’s a new global space race underway — between the United States, China, Russia… and unexpectedly, South Africa. But this time, the race isn’t about planting flags or sending astronauts. It’s about turning the Moon into a giant listening device using Radio Astronomy Telescopes — capable of detecting signals from the very beginning of the universe. Scientists believe the Moon could hold the key to answering some of the biggest unanswered questions in physics: How did the universe begin? What is dark matter? And are we alone? The reason everyone is trying to do this? Lies in a simple problem: Earth is noisy. Our atmosphere blocks certain radio signals travelling through space, and billions of electronic devices generate constant interference. In other words, scientists are trying to hear a whisper… in the middle of a stadium. But just 384,000 kilometres away, the Moon offers something unique: silence. With no atmosphere and minimal interference, it provides a rare opportunity to detect faint signals that have travelled billions of years — clues to what astronomers call “first light,” the moment the first stars formed after the Big Bang. At the centre of this mission is Carla Mitchell, an unlikely space pioneer based in Cape Town. Not an astrophysicist, but an economist working at the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, Carla has spent more than a decade chasing an idea many believed was impossible: placing radio astronomy instruments on the Moon. Her solution is deceptively simple. Instead of one massive telescope, Carla has designed small, spherical antennas — each about 30 centimetres wide — that can survive the unpredictable conditions of lunar landing. She calls them “Moon B.A.L.L.S.” — Bounced African Low Lunar Spheres. The design solves one of space exploration’s biggest challenges: landing. Traditional instruments can fail if they tip or land incorrectly. A sphere works no matter how it touches down. Her long-term vision is bold: to place dozens of these spheres across the Moon’s surface, allowing them to work together as a single, powerful telescope array — potentially the first of its kind on another world. And the ideal location? The far side of the Moon. Because the Moon is tidally locked, one side always faces Earth. The far side never does — making it naturally shielded from our planet’s radio noise, and one of the quietest places in the solar system.
metadata.Summary: But getting there has always been the challenge: Lunar missions cost hundreds of millions of dollars — far beyond the reach of most research teams. Until now. In 2023, China issued a global call for scientific experiments to join its future lunar programme. Countries around the world applied — including South Africa. After two years of evaluation, Carla’s Africa2Moon project was selected to fly on China’s Chang’e-8 mission, scheduled for 2029. The prize: a free ride to the Moon. For the first time, South Africa will be able to send scientific instruments into space at no launch cost — turning Carla’s decade-long vision into a real mission. But the opportunity comes with pressure. At SARAO in Observatory, Cape Town, Carla and her team are now racing to assemble and test the first Moon Ball prototypes. Budgets are tight, timelines are critical, and much of the work relies on collaboration, donated components, and determination. Carte Blanche has secured access to this project at a pivotal moment — as Carla’s idea moves from theory to reality. We would have a front row seat to the assembly and go with a presenter to meet the team. Carla says we can go to the top of the telescope and do an interview with the presenter looking at the moon, while discussing her dream. “People imagine huge telescopes,” Carla explains. “But our instruments are small. The Moon Balls are about thirty centimetres across — simple spherical antennas that can work no matter how they land.” For this initial mission, only three of the spherical antennas will be sent — a proof of concept. If successful, it could pave the way for a much larger array on future missions. With visuals from SARAO and the SKA telescope array (which Carte Blanche has reported on before), alongside NASA’s lunar archive and international launch footage, the story offers both scale and intimacy: a global race to the Moon… driven by one woman’s persistence. Because if this mission succeeds, Carla Mitchell’s small metal spheres — built in a lab in Cape Town — could help humanity listen back to the very first moments of the universe. “The first words spoken by God in the Bible are ‘Let there be light.’ In a way, that’s what we’re looking for — the first light in the universe, the first stars being born. One of the most exciting discoveries in radio astronomy is about trying to detect what we call ‘first light.’” And after more than a decade chasing the idea, she still looks up at the Moon with the same thought. “Sometimes I look up at the Moon and think — my balls are going to be there one day. I’ve been praying for this on my knees for years.” And in doing so, mark Africa’s first step onto another world.
